newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria urged not to sell $2 bln Iraqi debt.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria urged not to sell $2 bln Iraqi debt.

text.p: Bulgaria risks losing preferential conditions on the Iraqi market if it agrees to sell a $2-billion Baghdad debt to a third party, an official said on Wednesday.

"The Iraqi debt is not worth much at the moment. Bulgaria could get one quarter of its value at the most but lose a lot more in preferences in Iraq," Vassil Vassilev, chairman of the Bulgarian-Iraqi consortium told a news conference.

The debt, which totals about $1.5 billion plus interest, was accumulated between 1982 and 1990. Bulgaria, like other countries in Eastern Europe, supplied Baghdad with arms and other goods in return for crude oil during the Iran-Iraq war.
Trade was cut off after the United Nations Security Council imposed sanctions on Iraq for its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

Under an agreement signed in 1990, Iraq was to cover part of its debt by supplying Bulgaria with 4.75 million tonnes of crude oil by 1994. However, the embargo interrupted the deal after the first oil shipment worth $144 million was sent.

The United Nations approved a contract last year under which Bulgaria's chemical and oil trading firm, Himimport, can buy oil from Iraq under the UN resolution allowing Baghdad to sell oil to buy food and medicines.
Under the deal Himimport can buy 15,000 barrels per day.
The deal also provides an opportunity for Bulgarian firms to export drugs and pharmaceuticals, medical equipment, pumps and farming equipment, said Vassilev.
"Dozens of contracts were signed and are expected to produce results in the next few weeks," said Vassilev.
But local media said an unidentified third country has shown interest in acquiring the Iraqi debt in return for grain supplies.
And Bulgaria said it will import grain after uncontrolled exports and a bad harvest depleted its grain supplies.
